topics.title: Chapter 18 — SELinux in Practice
topics.summary: HarborWorks moves static web content from a distribution directory to /srv/harbor/site. The files are readable by the web worker, yet requests fail. The correct response is not “SELinux is broken.” The system has a policy describing which types of content the web service may read; the move may have changed the labels that express that intent.

topics.title: 18.1 Why SELinux Exists
topics.summary: Ordinary permissions answer whether a user or group may access an object. A compromised service still acts with its assigned identity, so every file readable by that identity can become part of the attack surface. SELinux can impose an additional policy boundary on the service’s domain.

blocks.text: Mandatory access control means the policy is enforced independently of a file owner’s ordinary discretionary permission choices. A user cannot necessarily make a file accessible to a confined service merely by running chmod 777.

Access normally must satisfy all relevant layers: path traversal, Unix mode or ACL rules, mount properties, SELinux policy, and possibly service sandboxing. A denial at any one can stop the operation. This layered model explains why fixing a Unix group can leave an SELinux problem unchanged and vice versa.

Compare credentials, file modes, and SELinux context.

id
ls -lZ /etc/passwd

blocks.text: getenforce reports the current enforcement mode. setenforce changes between enforcing and permissive at runtime where SELinux is enabled. It does not turn a disabled system into a fully enabled and correctly labeled one.

topics.title: 18.14 Why Disabling SELinux Is Usually the Wrong Fix
topics.summary: Disabling SELinux removes a boundary from the whole host and conceals the mismatch that caused the failure. It also turns future troubleshooting into a different environment from the supported baseline. The service may appear repaired while its access becomes broader than intended.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
lab_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$lab_dir"' EXIT
cd -- "$lab_dir"
dac=allow; object_type=default_t; permitted_type=httpd_sys_content_t
test "$dac" = allow
test "$object_type" != "$permitted_type"
printf 'DAC permits; type mismatch remains\n'
